analysis.one_liner: Slashes taxes on business owners and repeals the estate tax on large inheritances.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with zero cosponsors: referred to House Ways and Means in May 2022, it never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would sharply expand the tax deduction for business income: it would nearly triple the deduction (from 20% to 43% of business profits), make it permanent, remove the limit tied to wages the business pays, and extend it to every kind of business except regular employment — so law firms, hedge funds, and medical practices would qualify, not just shops and manufacturers. It would also shield corporate restructurings from tax when the owners don't change, and repeal the estate tax outright while letting inherited assets keep their tax-free 'stepped-up' value. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits: The largest gains would go to owners of profitable pass-through businesses — partnerships, S corporations, and sole proprietorships — especially high earners, because removing the wage limitation and the exclusion for professional-service firms lets lawyers, hedge fund managers, doctors, and consultants claim a deduction that shrinks their top rate toward the 21% corporate rate. Owners of large estates would gain the most in absolute terms: with the estate tax repealed after 2022 and the stepped-up basis retained, appreciated assets passed to heirs would escape both the estate tax and capital gains tax. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Owners of profitable businesses and large-estate heirs

how_it_helps.text: Makes the qualified business income deduction permanent by striking the provision that ends it, and raises the deduction from 20% to 43% of business profits (47% after 2025), targeting a top rate of 21% on that income. [S2] [S3]
Repeals the limit based on wages paid, so owners of businesses with few employees — such as professional practices and investment firms — can claim the full deduction. [S2] [S3]

Redefines a qualified business to mean anything except working as an employee, extending the deduction to law firms, hedge funds, medical groups, and other high-earning professional-service businesses that current law excludes. [S2] [S3]
Declares that changing a corporation's legal structure is not a taxable event when the owners, ownership shares, and assets stay the same. [S3]
Repeals the estate tax for decedents dying after 2022 while retaining the step-up in basis on inherited assets. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the cost would fall on the federal Treasury, and therefore on ordinary taxpayers either through higher future taxes, higher deficits, or cuts to public programs. The estate tax repeal would concentrate relief on estates above the taxable threshold, which affects only a small fraction of families, and combined with retained stepped-up basis, large appreciated fortunes would largely escape tax at transfer. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers through lost federal revenue

drawbacks.text: Repealing the limits and exclusions in current law extends a deduction pitched as small-business relief to some of the highest-earning pass-through owners, such as hedge funds and law partners, at a cost of tens of billions in revenue. [S2] [S3]

Repealing the estate tax while keeping stepped-up basis would let the largest inherited fortunes go untaxed at transfer, since neither the estate tax nor a capital gains tax would ever apply to the appreciation. [S3]
The revenue loss would be permanent and structural, since the bill makes the enlarged deduction permanent rather than temporary. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some genuinely small business owners would keep more of their profits, and a permanent deduction gives tax planning certainty. But the design is weighted toward the top: tripling the deduction, removing the wage test, and covering professional-service firms directs most of the benefit to high-income owners, and estate tax repeal on top of that is a pure transfer to heirs of very large estates. The public cost in revenue is large and permanent, while the benefit to a typical small business is comparatively modest.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in May 2022, attracted no cosponsors, and the committee never took it up, so it simply expired when the Congress ended in January 2023. [S4] [S5]

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs (R-AZ) introduced the bill on May 17, 2022 and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means. [S1] [S5]
No member of either party cosponsored it. [S4]
The House committee took no further action on the bill, and no vote was ever held in either chamber before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing tax structure stayed in place, so ordinary taxpayers avoided the cost of the proposed cuts; the proposed beneficiaries — high-income business owners and large-estate heirs — gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; no tax cuts were enacted

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Ways and Means Committee.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by a Democrat in the 117th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in May 2022 and took no further action — no markup, hearing, or vote — through the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: One House Republican sponsored the bill and no member of either party cosponsored it, so it never drew enough support to reveal a partisan split. [S4]

industries.industry: High-income pass-through business owners (hedge funds, law firms, medical practices)
industries.note: The bill would nearly triple their deduction, remove the wage-based limit, and sweep in professional-service firms now excluded, cutting their top rate toward 21%. Their gain comes directly out of federal revenue that ordinary taxpayers would otherwise keep. [S2] [S3]

Repealing the estate tax after 2022 while keeping stepped-up basis means the largest inherited fortunes would owe neither estate tax nor capital gains tax on appreciation. The benefit concentrates at the very top of the wealth distribution. [S2] [S3]

Genuinely small firms would also get a larger, permanent deduction, though the design channels the biggest dollars to high-earning owners. The public cost of the cuts is borne diffusely by all taxpayers. [S2] [S3]
Converting a corporation to another structure without changing owners or assets would no longer be a taxable event, removing tax friction from corporate form changes. [S3]
